source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping (Exp 1)
finding: People who read a base and target story judged a fact that fit a shared causal system as a better part of the analogy than an equally good fact outside that system. A control group that read only the target showed no such preference.
numbers: N=48 undergraduates, 4 passages. Rating of contribution to the analogy: shared-system fact 6.28 vs different-system fact 4.89 (7-point scale); target-only group 5.22 vs 5.31. Choice task: shared-system choices out of 4 = 3.17 (analogy) vs 2.0 (target-only), F(1,44)=18.43, p<.001. Per passage, analogy group chose the shared-system fact 67% to 92%, target-only 42% to 54%; Fisher test significant for 3 of 4 passages.
limits: Stories were hand built with causal antecedents; a one-to-one match to the causal system was always available. One passage did not reach significance. Subjects first listed correspondences, which may have pushed them to process structure.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a mapping scorer should reward a fact more if it hangs on a matched causal parent. The target-only control is the model for our own test: show the same facts without the analogy and check that the preference vanishes.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping (Exp 2)
finding: When asked which of two base facts would be true of the target, people chose the one that followed from the shared causal system, though both were plausible. The effect held in the choice task but was uneven across passages.
numbers: N about 32 (F df 1,28). Mean shared-system choices out of 4: 2.9 (analogy) vs 1.8 (target-only), F(1,28)=16.43, p<.001. Only 2 of 4 passages differed reliably: analogy group 87% and 69% vs target-only 44% and 25% (Fisher, p<.05). Other two passages: 62% and 75% vs 69% and 44%, not significant.
limits: Half the passages showed no reliable group difference. Authors blame a possibly biased key fact and misread base causal information. Small N per cell.
agent_relevance: Effect is real on average but passage dependent. A scorer based on systematicity should be a prior, not a decider, and be checked against content plausibility.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping (Exp 3)
finding: In a free prediction task (key facts removed from the target) analogy readers wrote more predictions that tied into the shared system than into the unshared one. One passage went the other way.
numbers: N=48. Shared minus different-system predictions written: 0.92 (analogy) vs 0.13 (target-only), F(1,44)=5.15, p<.05. Choice task: 1.875 vs 1.0 of 3, F(1,44)=13.15, p=.001. For two passages 66% of analogy subjects chose the shared-system fact vs 8% and 33% of target-only; for Passage 2 the split was 54% vs 58%, no effect.
limits: Passage 2 failed in both tasks. Authors blame subjects misrepresenting the base causal chain. Effect size on production is small (under one item per person).
agent_relevance: A cheap check for our agent: before copying a base relation into a target, ask whether its causal parent also holds in the target. The failure case shows the base must first be represented correctly (G2, G3).

source: Gentner & Toupin (1986) Systematicity and surface similarity in the development of analogy
finding: Children acted out a story and then re-enacted it with new characters. Systematic (explicit causal) stories helped transfer in 8 to 10 year olds, mainly when the new characters were cross-mapped. Younger children (4 to 6) did not gain reliably.
numbers: N=72 children, 36 aged 4-6 and 36 aged 8-10. 2x2x3 ANOVA: systematicity F(1,68)=6.28, p<.05; age F(1,68)=14.93, p<.001; mapping condition F(2,136)=29.01; systematicity x mapping F(2,136)=3.89, p<.05. Older group: t(34)=2.48, p<.01; younger group t(34)=1.08, NS. Systematicity helped only in the hardest (similar-but-swapped object) condition. Everyone was near perfect when objects matched in kind.
limits: No significant age x systematicity interaction (authors' own footnote), so 'only older children benefit' is not established. Effect confined to the hardest mapping. Authors cannot separate a competence limit from missing knowledge of the relations. Adult version only mentioned as preliminary.
agent_relevance: Shows systematicity acts as an error check during mapping: higher-order information lets a mapper catch a wrong object assignment. It matters most when surface cues mislead, the cross-mapped case an agent will meet.

source: Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness (Exp 1)
finding: Soundness and retrieval split apart. Analogy matches (shared causal structure, different objects) were rated much more sound than surface matches, but surface matches were recalled far more often one week later.
numbers: N=30 MIT students, 18 story sets. Soundness: analogy M=4.40 vs surface M=2.80 vs first-order-only M=2.74, F(2,58)=70.51, p<.0001. Proportion recalled: surface .78, analogy .44, first-order-only .25, F(2,58)=75.45.
limits: Story pairs are text; matches built by authors. Memory test after a delay with 18 originals. Relational remindings are not zero (.44), so access is poor but not absent.
agent_relevance: Warning for O7: the pull to a memory that looks alike is strong and is the wrong signal. Score a mapping on structure after retrieval; do not treat the retrieval rank as evidence of a good analogy.

source: Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness (Exp 2, 2x2 design)
finding: Crossing relational and object similarity showed that soundness tracks relational (higher-order) overlap while recall tracks object overlap. Adding object matches did not clearly raise soundness.
numbers: N=36 for reminding, 20 for ratings. Soundness: literal similarity 4.50, analogy 4.09, surface 3.40, first-order-only 2.88; relational main effect F(1,19)=85.78, p<.0001; object effect F(1,19)=7.01, p<.02. Recall: literal .56, surface .53, analogy .12, first-order-only .09; object effect F(1,35)=108.73; relational effect F=.89, NS. Correlation of soundness ratings with reminding r(78)=.008. Literal vs analogy soundness not reliably different (4.41 vs 4.16 in the discussion).
limits: Object similarity had a small but reliable soundness effect here (p<.02), less clean than Exp 1. Ratings came from a separate group of 20 Hampshire students.
agent_relevance: A large, clean dissociation. Supports a scoring rule that weights higher-order overlap and gives object overlap little weight for soundness.

source: Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness (Exp 4 and MAC/FAC simulation)
finding: A follow-up showed the weak relational retrieval was at access, not encoding. Subjects with relationally similar probes failed to find the base even though they had stored it. A two-stage model (cheap content-vector filter, then structure mapping) reproduced the human order.
numbers: N=27 (14 and 13). Group 1 (surface-similar probes, forced choice) picked the right base 82% of the time (16.46 of 20, chi-square p<.0001). Group 2 (relationally similar probes) picked it 55% (11 of 20), chance. Simulation: base passed both stages with proportion 1.0 for literal, .89 for surface, .67 for analogy probes.
limits: Simulation matched ordering only (ordinal), with hand-coded story representations. Result depends on how much surface detail the encoding holds (see Specificity Conjecture).
agent_relevance: Supports a two-pass design: broad cheap recall of candidates, then an explicit structure check. A design choice for O7, not yet tested by us.

source: Forbus & Gentner (1989) Structural evaluation of analogies: what counts?
finding: Sensitivity analysis of how to score a mapping for systematicity. A cascade that passes a share of each relation's score down to its arguments (trickle-down) fits human soundness data even when descriptions are mostly surface detail. Scoring by relation order, or combining evidence by Dempster-Shafer, gets swamped by surface matches.
numbers: 343 parameter points per algorithm; 6,174 structural evaluations. AddMax normalisation with Trickle-Down in [4,16], Same-Predicate in [0.001,0.01], Same-Function in [0.0001,0.01]: every point fit the human ordering. Fail: Trickle-Down 1.0 or less, Same-Predicate 0.3 or more. Dempster-Shafer fit only top-heavy (mostly abstract) descriptions. Order-scoring failed on bottom-heavy descriptions.
limits: Fit measured on three story triads, coded as 0 to 3 agreement with human ordering. The 'Specificity Conjecture' (human memories are mostly surface detail) is a conjecture. Structural score only; no goals or context.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete, code-checkable scoring rule for O7: weight a matched fact by the matched structure above it, with a strong cascade and a low baseline for flat attribute matches. A raw count of matched facts will be swamped by surface detail.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus & Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: SME implements systematicity locally: each matched relation passes 80% of its belief to the matches of its arguments, and a mapping's score is the sum of its match scores. Deeper shared structure scores higher than the same number of flat matches. Under free-for-all rules (no identity constraint) it still picks supersets of the standard mapping but adds spurious pairs.
numbers: Trickle-down factor 0.8; initial score 0.2 in the free-for-all rule set. Free-for-all on water/heat: 74 match hypotheses, 26 mappings, 4 tied for the top score (3.71). Runtime: a flat baseball analogy could not be mapped in hours; a PHINEAS problem took 53 minutes and fell to 34 seconds after adding systematic structure. Typical cost roughly quadratic.
limits: Symbolic input only; representation is hand written. Authors argue against a purely goal-driven (pragmatic) rival (Holyoak) but give no head-to-head human test here. Dempster-Shafer scoring was dropped for numerical problems.
agent_relevance: Systematicity is also a search pruner: structure makes mapping tractable. For an agent working from raw text, the first job is to produce a structured description; the score follows from it.

source: Colhoun & Gentner (2009) Inference processes in causal analogies (Study 1A, 1B)
finding: Replicated the Lee & Holyoak finding that similarity ratings and effect-inference ratings come apart when a preventive cause is shared. Then showed the dissociation disappears when overall inductive strength is measured over all candidate inferences, which follows similarity.
numbers: 1A: N=70 (36 similarity, 34 inference). Similarity: GGP 7.53 > GG 6.35 > GP 5.01, F(2,286)=44.4. Effect inference: GG 89.4 > GGP 74.4 > GP 46.1, F(2,270)=164.6. 1B: N=22 (3 excluded); proportion of inferences endorsed ordered GGP > GG > GP, F(2,174)=142.3, p<.0001.
limits: Authors sit on one side of a theory dispute. Choosing 'mean over all inferences' as the measure is their choice. The endorsement measure changed the task format.
agent_relevance: A rival (causal-model) account says one inference can be less likely while the analogy is more similar. Practical lesson: judge a mapping by the whole set of candidate inferences, then judge each inference in the target.

source: Colhoun & Gentner (2009) Inference processes in causal analogies (Study 2, 3)
finding: Whether the causal relations were given in the base or in the target made no difference to effect inference. A simulation that ran SME and then a simple causal calculation reproduced the human data.
numbers: Study 2: N=32 (4 excluded). Group effect F(2,56)=.55, NS; interaction F(4,56)=.77, NS; target type F(2,56)=56.1, p<.0001. Only the group given base relations plus the effect rated the GP target higher. Study 3: SME plus causal calculation 'closely' matched human data (no fit statistic in the text read).
limits: Small cells (8 per group). Simulation fit is qualitative. Conference proceedings paper, not a full journal report.
agent_relevance: Suggests a two-step pipeline: map first (structure), then evaluate each projected inference with a causal check in the target. Fits the schema's split between a code step and a model step.

source: Lee & Holyoak (2007) Causal models guide analogical inference
finding: Rival view. Removing a matching preventive cause from the target lowered similarity yet raised inductive strength. The authors read this as showing people build and run a causal model of the target, not just copy structure.
numbers: Exp 1: N=42. Similarity: N1N2P 7.58, N1N2 4.77, N1P 5.09. Inductive strength: N1N2 58.57, N1N2P 33.60, N1P 35.32; argument type F(2,36)=8.44, p<.01. Exp 2: N=60 UCLA students (generative and preventive conditions).
limits: A single inference (the effect) is the measure; Colhoun & Gentner (2009) argue the whole inference set is the right measure. Animal descriptions are synthetic.
agent_relevance: The strongest published rival to a pure systematicity score. It argues for a causal check after mapping, which our design already requires (G2, G3).

source: Myers & Gentner (2017) Analogical inferences in causal systems
finding: A test designed to discriminate the two accounts. When the base showed that a generative cause outweighed two preventive causes, people carried that higher-order relation to the target, raising effect inference, not just transferring probabilities of single causes.
numbers: N=40 recruited, 32 analysed. Effect inference: G1P1P2 base 62.28 (SD 19.84) vs G1G2P1 base 47.28 (SD 17.49), t(31)=3.44, p<.005. Similarity 6.25 vs 5.78, t(31)=1.54, p=.13 (same direction, not significant).
limits: Same lab as the structure-mapping side. Small N, undergraduates, synthetic animals, proceedings paper. Experiment 2 (familiar vs novel preventive feature) only partly read.
agent_relevance: Supports mapping relations between relations ('stronger than') as units that transfer. A mapping that stores only first-order links would lose this.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: Review tying together evidence for systematicity, including the time course: under about 700 to 1000 ms deadlines people rely on local matches, at longer deadlines on relational matches. It also restates that retrieval is surface weighted while soundness is structure weighted, and a transparency effect in transfer.
numbers: Clement & Gentner: key fact tied to the matched antecedent predicted more than twice as often. Response deadline of about 700 to 1000 ms flips preference from local to relational matches (Goldstone & Medin 1994; Ratcliff & McKoon 1989). Gentner et al. 1993 restated.
limits: Narrative review by authors of the theory. Counter-evidence (e.g. Hammond, Seifert & Gray 1991 on retrieval) is only named. The deadline claim comes from other papers I did not read.
agent_relevance: Time pressure favors local matches. A fast agent pass will over-trust surface similarity; give the structure check its own step and budget.

source: Gentner (1983) Structure-mapping: a theoretical framework for analogy
finding: Defines the systematicity principle: a predicate that belongs to a mappable system of mutually connected relations is more likely to be imported than an isolated one. Reports an interpretation study: analogy interpretations were mostly relational, and aptness tracked how relational the interpretation was.
numbers: No sample size recoverable from the text read. Study: written interpretations of comparisons such as 'a cigarette is like a time bomb' rated by naive judges as attribute or relation; relations dominated for analogies but not for object descriptions; aptness correlated with relational content. Example: 'more massive than' maps in the solar system/atom analogy, 'hotter than' does not.
limits: A theory paper; the cited study is described briefly (Gentner 1980 manuscript) with no numbers. Systematicity is a stated preference defined by connectivity, not a measured constant.
agent_relevance: Source of the idea to score by connected higher-order structure. Treat the principle as an empirical prior, not a law.

source: Gentner & Forbus (2025) The Structure-Mapping Engine: a multidecade interaction between psychology and AI
finding: Latest summary from the theory's authors. SME has three stages (local matches, structurally consistent clusters rated with a systematicity bias, then merged mappings). They state SME captures the preference for systematic sets and the finding that people project inferences from a more systematic case to a less systematic one. On LLMs they say it is open whether generative models can do analogical processing without a symbolic partner.
numbers: Cites Bowdle & Gentner 1997 (direction of inference) and Clement & Gentner 1991. Mapping is NP-complete in general, which SME avoids by local construction. Mentions vector embeddings inside SME's evaluation (Liang et al. 2016) and LLM-assisted learning by reading (Nakos & Forbus 2023).
limits: Short review; no new data. Authors are partisans.
agent_relevance: Authors agree the LLM question is open. A hybrid (LLM extracts structure, code maps and scores) matches their own suggestion and our G5.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (story analogies)
finding: GPT-3 chose the story sharing causal (higher-order) relations with the source above chance for near analogies but not for far (cross-domain) analogies. College students clearly beat it. GPT-4 did better in a first check.
numbers: 18 source stories from Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus 1993; 72 problems; humans N=54 UCLA students. Humans: near t(53)=21.5, far t(53)=16.7 against chance. GPT-3: near binomial p=.0039, far p=.065 (not significant). Human vs GPT-3 odds ratio 0.37, p=.0003, CI [0.21, 0.63]. 15 of 54 students were right on every trial. GPT-4: near close to perfect, far more reliable than GPT-3 (Supplementary Fig. 6).
limits: Materials may be in training data (authors say no evidence found). Contested by later work. GPT-4 tested by hand through the ChatGPT interface.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of the systematicity-based preference. The preference is present in near stories; the weakness is in far, cross-domain pairs, where a mapping check would add the most.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (other tasks)
finding: On letter strings, Raven-like digit matrices and four-term verbal analogies GPT-3 matched or beat human averages. It failed to use an analogy when distractor stories were present unless prompted, and could name correspondences it could not use to solve a physical problem.
numbers: Verbal: UCLA VAT humans N=57, Sternberg & Nigro N=20, Jones et al. N=241; SAT items 374, GPT-3 above the estimated average high school student. Letter strings: humans N=57. Radiation problem: GPT-3 gave the convergence solution after the general story but not after two distractor stories until prompted.
limits: Zero-shot, text only; open question whether tasks were in training data. Robustness checks by others show sharp drops on variants (next lines).
agent_relevance: Accuracy on benchmark analogies is a weak sign of mapping ability. Needed: tests with surface changed and structure held.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models (story analogies)
finding: Re-ran the story analogy test. GPT-4 had a strong answer-order bias (humans none), and accuracy fell when the correct target was paraphrased to remove sentence-by-sentence overlap with the source. Part of the success seems to rest on surface alignment, in humans too.
numbers: 18 'far' problems. GPT-4 correct-first 1.0 (18/18), correct-second 0.72 (13/18); total 0.86 (31/36). Webb et al. GPT-4: 0.89 first, 0.61 second, 0.75 total. Humans (N=245 Prolific): 0.78 both orders, total 0.78 (564/720). Paraphrased correct target: GPT-4 0.86 to 0.72 (26/36); humans 0.78 to 0.70 (503/720).
limits: Only 18 problems; the larger GPT-4 drop may not be significant (authors say so). Paraphrase written by the authors. One model family (GPT-4-0613).
agent_relevance: A confound for any systematicity test: the correct answer often shares sentence order and wording with the source. Our tests must shuffle order and paraphrase. Also G4: position bias is noise; randomize and average both orders in code.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models (letter strings and matrices)
finding: Replicated Webb et al. on original letter-string and digit-matrix problems, then showed GPT models drop sharply on variants that keep the same relational structure (fictional alphabets, moved blank cell) while humans do not.
numbers: Letter strings, zero-generalization accuracy over all alphabets: humans 0.754 [0.734,0.773], GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (263 human participants in the study). Matrices: humans digits 0.715, alt-blank 0.771, symbols 0.704; GPT-4 0.810, 0.477, 0.792 (GPT-3.5 0.813, 0.480, 0.790). Replication note: their humans scored higher than Webb's on zero-generalization problems.
limits: Zero-shot with simple prompts; no chain of thought or reasoning models. Webb et al. (2024) say the letter-string drop is a counting problem (next lines).
agent_relevance: Structure held, surface changed: the drop shows models lean partly on surface patterns. Our mapper should be tested the same way.

source: Hodel & West (2024) Response: emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Critique: the zero-shot claim is unproven because letter-string problems are discussed on the web and memorisation was not ruled out. ChatGPT could produce letter-string examples on request, which is weak evidence of exposure.
numbers: Mostly qualitative in the sections read. Additional human and model tests with letter-string variants are in an appendix (not read in detail).
limits: Argument about contamination, not a measurement of systematicity. Webb et al. reply that this kind of recall test is weak.
agent_relevance: Use items written after the model cutoff or generated fresh each run for our own scoring tests.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (reply)
finding: Reply arguing the failure on permuted alphabets is mostly counting: GPT-4 with code execution reached human-level accuracy, GPT-4 without code did not. Authors say the drop reflects an auxiliary task demand, not missing analogy.
numbers: Humans vs GPT-4: P=8.9e-13 (humans better); humans vs GPT-4 plus code: P=0.496 (no difference). Interval size 2 harder for humans (P=1.5e-11) and GPT-4 (P<2e-16), not significant with code (P=0.066). 46% of GPT-4's errors fit a valid alternative rule vs 39% in human data. Human N=99 and 97 in two conditions.
limits: Code execution is not human-like and is a different route. Used a stronger, later model. The two camps do not test the same stimuli in story form.
agent_relevance: Supports tool use for mechanical parts (indexing, counting) and the model for relation finding. Matches our rule that code does counting and ranking.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere & Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: New tasks with fresh stimuli that need re-representing words as features and mapping them to symbols. The best recent models (GPT-4, Claude 3, Llama 405B) reached human-level on many conditions, GPT-3 did poorly, but models reacted to control conditions (random source words, element order) differently from people.
numbers: Humans on Prolific compared with GPT-3, GPT-4, Claude 3, Llama 405B across semantic structure and semantic content studies. 'Match to reference' used since answers are not unique. Prompting variants moved performance from near 0 to 40% in one condition and 20% to 100% in another.
limits: Prompt sensitivity is very large, so cross-model rankings are fragile. Task is not the classic systematicity test; authors say structure mapping side-steps how representations are built.
agent_relevance: Newer models can map; prompt sensitivity is large. Two things to copy: run several prompt variants and compare in code, and expect representation building to be the weak step.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer & Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical reasoning on narratives
finding: Benchmark built on the surface vs system mapping distinction. Models do well when the analogy also shares surface features, and fail, often below chance, when they must prefer a far analogy (system mapping only) over a near distractor (surface only).
numbers: 1,096 triples. Humans 96% vs models 57% average. Near analogies: humans 97.9%, models 75.0%. Far analogies: humans 94.1%, models 39.6% (below the 50% chance line). Partitions (average over models): near analogy vs far disanalogy 76.9%, near vs near 73.2%, far vs far 45.3%, far analogy vs near disanalogy 33.9%. GPT-4 best at 68.1% average; SBERT 42.3% and about 1% when a far analogy must beat a near distractor. Asking explicitly for system mappings changed little. Step-by-step prompts helped more than plain examples.
limits: Narratives are short, built from the ePiC proverb set, near analogies partly LLM-written. Some partitions can be solved by picking the less similar story, a shortcut the authors note. Human N not read.
agent_relevance: The clearest LLM test matching 'prefer systematic over surface'. Result: models prefer surface. A systematicity scorer run in code on extracted relation graphs is a plausible fix, not yet tested by us.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: deriving story-level analogies from LLMs
finding: Large corpus of story pairs rated for entity similarity and relation similarity (an extension of structure mapping). Multiple-choice analogy identification is hard for LLMs, which are often lured by surface-similar hard negatives.
numbers: 24K story pairs. Multiple choice (4 options): random 25%, humans 85.7%, retrieval baseline (Sultan & Shahaf) 44.9%, FlanT5-xxl 45.4%, LLaMa-65B 28.6%, ChatGPT 32.4%, GPT-3.5 37.1%. Best LLM about 37.7 points under humans. Annotator agreement (Fleiss kappa) 47% entity, 42% relation (moderate). Few-shot on this data raised generation quality (+28.4% and +27.5% for LLaMa).
limits: Stories mostly LLM-generated; labels by crowd workers with moderate agreement. Model scores come from a garbled table extraction, so treat each to about a point.
agent_relevance: Another independent sign that models over-weight surface, and that human-rated relation similarity is noisy: our scorer needs repeated runs and agreement checks.

source: Stevenson et al. (2023) Do large language models solve verbal analogies like children do?
finding: On Dutch children's A:B::C:? analogies, LLMs scored about like 11-year-olds, but most correct answers could be reached by association with C, and performance dropped 1 to 2 age-years once association was controlled. Authors conclude models tend to use association like young children.
numbers: 14,006 children aged 7-12, 622 analogies after item filters; 6 LLMs. GPT-3 and XLM-V slightly above the 11-year-old level, M-GPT near the 7-year-old level. GPT-4 solved over 70% with only the C term shown (contamination or association).
limits: Pre-registered, but Dutch single-word analogies, not structured systems. Association vs relation is a simpler contrast than systematicity.
agent_relevance: A control to copy: remove one term and see if the answer stays the same. If so, the model used an association, not the mapping.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Analogy used as a prompting method, not as a test of structure mapping: the model writes its own related solved examples first. Reported gains over zero-shot and few-shot chain of thought on math and code.
numbers: Benchmarks GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces, BIG-Bench. The table text extracted garbled; the main claim is gains over 0-shot CoT and manual 5-shot CoT across the models tested. I do not record exact deltas.
limits: It does not test whether the generated examples share higher-order structure with the problem, so it says nothing about systematicity. Quality of self-generated examples is unchecked.
agent_relevance: Partial fit to O7: self-generated examples need a structure check (G2, G3). Without it, retrieval pulls surface neighbours.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini & Moskvichev (2023) Comparing humans, GPT-4 and GPT-4V on abstraction and reasoning tasks
finding: Only the title and abstract opening were seen. Uses ConceptARC to test whether GPT-4 grasps core concepts robustly. A pointer, not evidence.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract; do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a later pass on abstraction-level mapping.
